title: Species and groups disappear gradually, place by place, not by global catastrophes

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species and groups disappear gradually, place by place, not by global catastrophes

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species and groups of species generally become extinct gradually, one after another, disappearing first from one place, then another, and finally from the world, rather than being swept away together by catastrophes.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: species and groups of species gradually disappear, one after another, first from one spot, then from another, and finally from the world.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On Extinction”. Scope: extinction of species and groups, especially in the Tertiary

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-07: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.82

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Global fossil occurrences directly address extinction tempo and spatial sequence. Known sampling effects complicate direction, but event-specific models can distinguish many gradual and catastrophic patterns.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure the temporal and geographic sequence of last occurrences for species and higher taxa, and quantify clustering at extinction horizons. Compare range contraction and staggered losses with globally synchronous abrupt disappearance.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Dating precision differs among regions.

The Signor-Lipps effect makes abrupt extinction appear gradual.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Global event horizons versus staggered regional last appearances are measurable with occurrence data and independent section ages. Methods that put confidence intervals on last appearances reduce, without removing, the tendency of incomplete ranges to look gradual. The usual pattern across the later record can be scored even though place-by-place paths exist only for better-sampled groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare last-appearance timing of species and genera across regions, and the share of extinctions that fall in globally correlated short intervals versus staggered regional losses. Globally synchronous removal as the usual pattern would challenge the claim; regionally staggered losses outside those intervals would support it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Geographic coverage is too thin to follow most individual species from place to place.

The Signor-Lipps effect smears an abrupt extinction backward so that it looks gradual.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If Tertiary extinctions were gradual and place-by-place rather than catastrophic, the last occurrences of extinct genera should be spread across many Tertiary stages rather than concentrated in one or two, and genera recorded on several continents should usually disappear from those continents at demonstrably different times, more often than genera killed in the known K-Pg catastrophe.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Genus-resolved PBDB occurrences of Mollusca and Mammalia from the Campanian to the Pliocene were downloaded for each of nine PBDB continents. For each genus flagged extinct in PBDB taxonomy, the last occurrence (smallest minimum age) was located and its age midpoint assigned to an ICS stage; genera whose database-wide last appearance is younger than the Tertiary were excluded. Clause A measured the concentration of Tertiary last occurrences across the 17 Tertiary stages (largest single-stage share; number of ranked stages needed to reach 50%). Clause B took Tertiary-extinct genera with >= 2 occurrences on each of >= 2 continents and called their disappearance staggered when the first-vanishing continent's last-occurrence age range lies entirely before the last-vanishing continent's; the same statistic was computed for genera with a Maastrichtian last occurrence as a K-Pg catastrophe control.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Two groups are analysed separately with Paleobiology Database genus-level occurrences from the Campanian through the Pliocene: Mollusca and Mammalia. Clause A (no catastrophic concentration): among PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence (midpoint of its age range) falls in the Tertiary (Danian to Piacenzian, 17 ICS stages), the single stage holding the most last occurrences holds < 1/3 of them, and at least 4 stages are needed to accumulate 50% of them when stages are ranked by count. Clause B (place by place): among those Tertiary-extinct genera that have >= 2 occurrences on each of >= 2 continents (PBDB continent codes), the fraction whose regional last occurrences are staggered (the earliest-vanishing continent's last-occurrence minimum age is older than the last-vanishing continent's last-occurrence maximum age, i.e. non-overlapping age ranges) is > 0.5 AND exceeds the same fraction computed for the K-Pg control set (PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence midpoint falls in the Maastrichtian, using Campanian-Maastrichtian occurrences). A clause passes only if it passes in both groups. Verdict 'supports' if both clauses pass, 'mixed' if exactly one passes, 'refutes' if neither passes.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Clause A fails if, in either group, one Tertiary stage holds >= 1/3 of the genus last occurrences or <= 3 stages hold 50% of them. Clause B fails if, in either group, the staggered fraction is <= 0.5 or does not exceed the K-Pg control's staggered fraction (which would mean the apparent staggering is no greater than what incomplete sampling produces in a known simultaneous extinction). Both clauses failing refutes the claim; the K-Pg control itself is outside the claim's Tertiary scope and is used only as a sampling-artefact baseline.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: mean over the two groups of the fraction of multi-continent Tertiary-extinct genera with staggered regional last occurrences

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'species and groups of species' are tested at the genus level because genus-level identifications are far more complete and less affected by taxonomic noise in PBDB. 'Disappearing from one spot, then another' is read as non-overlapping last-occurrence age ranges on different continents (modern continents, PBDB cc codes). 'Swept away together by catastrophes' is read as a strong concentration of last occurrences in one or two stages. The Signor-Lipps effect makes any extinction look gradual and staggered in an incomplete record; the Maastrichtian (K-Pg) control set provides an empirical baseline for how staggered a real catastrophe looks in the same database, so clause B requires Tertiary staggering to exceed that baseline. Scope is the Tertiary, as Darwin stated; the K-Pg event itself is not used to judge the claim.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
Paleobiology Database occurrences, Mollusca and Mammalia, Campanian-Pliocene, genus-resolved, per continent

Paleobiology Database taxa with first/last appearance ages and extant flags (occs/taxa, show=app)

Paleobiology Database international time scale (scale 1) interval boundaries

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Regional staggering is only detectable at the resolution of the occurrence dating: when a genus's last occurrences on two continents are both dated only to the same stage (common for mammals, whose records are often dated to land-mammal ages spanning several stages, and for all Maastrichtian records in the control), the ranges overlap and the genus is scored 'not staggered'. The mammal result for clause B is therefore partly a dating-resolution result, and the K-Pg control's zero staggering reflects the same effect as much as the catastrophe itself.

The Mammalia K-Pg control set is empty (no extinct mammal genus with >= 2 Maastrichtian occurrences on each of two continents), so for mammals clause B rests only on the > 0.5 condition.

Genus last occurrences in PBDB are truncated by sampling (Signor-Lipps), so both the spread across stages and the regional staggering are biased toward looking gradual; the Maastrichtian control set calibrates this for clause B but not for clause A.

The Tertiary window ends at the Piacenzian; genera that actually died out in the Pleistocene but have no PBDB Pleistocene record are counted as Piacenzian extinctions, inflating the youngest stage.

Stage assignment uses the midpoint of the last occurrence's age range; poorly dated occurrences spanning several stages add noise to clause A.

Modern continents are used as 'places'; a genus vanishing from one basin while persisting in another on the same continent is not visible, which biases clause B toward 'not staggered'.

PBDB coverage is heavily weighted to Europe and North America; staggering between continents can reflect unequal sampling rather than real sequential disappearance.

The test is at genus level, not species level, and is confined to Darwin's stated Tertiary scope; the K-Pg (Maastrichtian) set shows what a catastrophic horizon looks like in the same data and is deliberately excluded from the verdict.
